facts.statement: Banking and the sources of regulation (courseware): banking in India is mainly governed by the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934; the Reserve Bank and the Government exercise control over banks from the opening to winding up by virtue of powers under these Acts. The regulatory provisions are not uniformly applicable to all banks: applicability depends on the constitution of the bank, that is, whether it is a statutory corporation, a banking company or a co-operative society. The definition of banking in Section 5(b) of the Banking Regulation Act: accepting, for the purpose of lending or investing, deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise. A bank therefore performs two essential functions: acceptance of deposits from the public and lending or investment of such deposits. Deposits may be repayable on demand or after a period as agreed; accepting deposits from the public does not mean the banker accepts from anyone who offers money (a banker can refuse to open accounts of undesirable persons and opening is subject to know-your-customer norms, which also require monitoring suspicious transactions for reporting under anti-money laundering and countering terrorism financing measures).

Deposits, non-banking entities and the licence (courseware): under Section 49A no person other than a banking company, the Reserve Bank, the State Bank of India or any other banking institution, firm or other person notified by the Central Government is authorised to accept for the payment of money any deposit withdrawable by cheque. Non-banking financial companies and some other firms and associations accept deposits from the public; acceptance by non-banking financial companies is regulated by the Reserve Bank under the Non-Banking Financial Companies Acceptance of Public Deposits (Reserve Bank) Directions, 1998 and other directions under Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act. A licence from the Reserve Bank under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act is necessary to commence or carry on the business of banking in India. Every banking company has to use the word bank as part of its name (Section 7) and no company other than a banking company can use the words bank, banker or banking as a part of its name; no firm, individual or group of individuals may use the words bank, banking or banker as a part of the name or for the purpose of its business. Subsidiaries of banks and associations of banks in certain cases, primary credit societies and a co-operative society formed for the protection of mutual interest of co-operative banks and any co-operative society formed by the employees of a banking company, not being a primary credit society, and the State Bank of India or nationalised banks are exempted from this restriction.

Permitted and prohibited business (courseware): the main business of banks is acceptance of deposits and lending or investing, but banks carry on many allied business activities. Activities permitted under Section 6(1) include dealing in bills of exchange (drawing, accepting, buying, selling, collecting), lending or advancing money, carrying on and transacting every kind of guarantee and indemnity business, managing, selling and realising any property which may come into the possession of the bank in satisfaction or part satisfaction of any of its claims, and others; the Central Government may notify other business under Section 6(1). Prohibited business (Section 8): a banking company shall not engage directly or indirectly in trading activities and shall not undertake trading risks; buying, selling or bartering of goods is prohibited; goods mean every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims, stocks, shares, money, bullion and specie and instruments referred to in Section 6(1). This does not prejudice business permitted under Section 6(1); a bank can realise securities given to it or held by it for a loan, if need arises for the realisation of the amount lent. It can also buy or sell or barter for others in connection with bills of exchange received for collection or negotiation and undertake the administration of estates as executor or trustee. Section 9 (disposal of non-banking assets): no banking company shall hold any immovable property howsoever acquired, except as required for its own use, for any period exceeding seven years from the acquisition thereof; the property shall be disposed of within such period or extended period; the Reserve Bank may extend the period by up to five years where it is satisfied that the extension would be in the interests of the depositors.

Constitution of banks (courseware): banks in India fall under one of the categories: a body corporate constituted under a special statute; a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956 (Companies Act, 2013) or a foreign company; or a co-operative society registered under a Central or state enactment. Public sector banks (other than the State Bank of India) are constituted under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts of 1970 and 1980: under Section 3 of these Acts the Central Government nationalised (took over the business of) certain banking companies and vested them in newly created statutory bodies (corresponding new banks). The State Bank of India was constituted under the State Bank of India Act, 1955 and the seven associate or subsidiary banks under the State Bank (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959; the seven subsidiaries and associates were merged with the State Bank of India, completed in the financial year 2017-18. Regional Rural Banks were constituted under the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976 and are governed by the statutes creating them as well as some provisions of the Banking Regulation Act and the Reserve Bank of India Act. Most private sector banks (including micro and small finance banks) are companies constituted under the Companies Act; foreign banks are foreign companies constituted under statutes abroad and treated as such under Section 2(42) of the Companies Act, 2013; certain provisions of the Companies Act apply as provided, and all foreign companies transacting banking in India are governed by the Banking Regulation Act and the RBI Act regarding their banking business.

Co-operative banks (courseware): a co-operative bank conducts ordinary banking business but is established on a co-operative basis. Co-operative credit institutions are urban co-operative banks (scheduled and non-scheduled, multi-state or single state) and rural co-operatives: long term (state co-operative agriculture and rural development banks and primary co-operative agriculture and rural development banks) and short term (state co-operative banks, district central co-operative banks and primary agricultural credit societies). If a co-operative bank operates in more than one state, the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act applies; otherwise the respective state Co-operative Societies Act applies. By the Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1965, certain provisions of the Banking Regulation Act and the RBI Act were extended to the co-operative banking sector (Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act with effect from 1965). Over the years problems in co-operative banks (the PMC Bank failure in Mumbai in 2019-20) led to the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020, in force from 29 September 2020 as stated in the courseware, giving the Reserve Bank more regulatory control over the management, capital, audit and liquidation of co-operative banks, including powers of supersession of the board and restructuring and the reconstruction of such banks. The amended Section 56 modifies references: banking company becomes co-operative bank, commencement of the Act becomes commencement of the Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, memorandum or articles become bye-laws, and Registrar of Companies becomes the Central or State Registrar of Co-operative Societies. Co-operative banks may raise capital through public or private issues of equity, preference shares and debentures but this does not affect the existing powers of the State Registrars. For co-operative banks registered under the deposit insurance and credit guarantee law the Reserve Bank can order winding up in specified circumstances. Control is dual: State Governments and the Registrar under the Co-operative Societies Act control formation, management and winding up; the Reserve Bank controls banking licensing and regulation of banking business.

Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (courseware): the Act was enacted to constitute the Reserve Bank, with the primary aim to regulate the issue of bank notes and to keep reserves to secure monetary stability and generally to operate the currency and credit system to the country advantage. It deals with the constitution, powers and functions of the Reserve Bank and does not directly deal with regulation of the banking system except for Section 42, which provides for cash reserves of scheduled banks to be kept with the Reserve Bank so as to regulate the credit system and ensure monetary stability; Section 18 provides for direct discount of bills of exchange and promissory notes. The general superintendence and direction of affairs is vested in the Central Board of Directors consisting of a Governor and not more than four deputy governors appointed by the Central Government; four directors nominated by the Central Government, one from each of the local boards; ten directors nominated by the Central Government; and two government officials nominated by the Government. A scheduled bank is one included in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, which includes only those banks that satisfy the criteria in Section 42(6)(a). Other sections: constitution (Section 3), capital (Section 4), management (Section 7), composition of the Central Board and term of office (Section 8), business the bank may transact (Section 17 and not transact Section 19), issue of bank notes (Section 22), power of the Central Government to supersede the Central Board (Section 30), and cash reserve requirement of scheduled banks (Section 42). The Reserve Bank acts as lender of last resort (an institution offering funds to banks or other financial institutions that are experiencing financial difficulty or are considered highly risky) under Sections 17 and 18. Non-banking financial company amendments in 2019 (Chapter VI of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019) gave the Reserve Bank powers to replace or supersede the board of a regulated non-banking financial company, remove or debar auditors, frame schemes for amalgamation, reconstruction or splitting into viable and non-viable businesses, and direct group company statements and inspection.

Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (courseware): a comprehensive legislation regulating banks, passed as the Banking Companies Act 1949 and in force from 16 March 1949; renamed the Banking Regulation Act from 1 March 1966; applied to Jammu and Kashmir from 1956; extended to co-operative banks in 1965 by adding Section 56. The Act covers the definition of banking, licensing, capital and reserve requirements, banking operations and management structure, liquidity provisions, bank inspection and the takeover, amalgamation and liquidation of banks. The Reserve Bank has powers to license banks, regulate shareholding and voting rights, supervise the appointment of the board and managers, regulate the operations, lay down instructions for audits, issue moratorium, mergers and liquidation, issue directives in the interest of public good and on banking policy and impose penalties. Amendments: the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2017 inserted Sections 35AA and 35AB empowering the Reserve Bank to issue directions to any banking company to initiate insolvency resolution in default cases under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016; the 2012 amendment set up the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund to take over inoperative deposit accounts not claimed or operated for ten years; the Reserve Bank conducts an annual financial inspection of banking companies under Section 35 and risk-based supervision through the Supervisory Program on Assessment of Risk and Capital. Objectives of the Banking Regulation Act: provide specific legislation to the business of banking in India; prevent bank failures by prescribing minimum capital requirements; ensure balanced development and growth of banking companies; give specific powers to the Reserve Bank; and safeguard the interest of depositors.

Reserve Bank and Government as regulators (courseware): the Reserve Bank is the regulator of banks and other financial institutions such as non-banking financial companies; the Department of Non-Banking Supervision is entrusted with regulation and supervision of non-banking financial companies under Chapter III B and C and Chapter V of the RBI Act. Major powers of the Reserve Bank as regulator and supervisor: power to issue banking licences; power of appointment and removal of managerial personnel or boards; power to regulate the business of banks; power to give directions; power to inspect and supervise banks; power regarding audit of banks; power to collect, collate and furnish credit information; power relating to moratorium, amalgamation and winding up; and power to impose penalties. The Government of India is the sole shareholder of the Reserve Bank; the Governor and members of the Central Board are appointed by the Government who also have powers to remove them. Under Section 7(1) of the RBI Act the Government can give directions to the Reserve Bank in the public interest in consultation with the Governor; the courseware notes this power was supposed to be used rarely and was first used in October 2018 when letters were sent on liquidity for non-banking financial companies, capital requirement for weak banks and lending to small enterprises. Government powers to influence Reserve Bank decisions include appellate authority in several matters: appeal against removal of managerial personnel (Section 10B and 36AA of the Banking Regulation Act); appeals against cancellation of a banking licence (Section 22) and refusal of a certificate on floating charges (Section 14A); suspension of operations or exemption from provisions of the Act (Sections 4 and 53 respectively) on recommendation of the Reserve Bank; notification of other business banks may engage in (Section 6(1)); rule making (Sections 52 and 45Y on preservation of records); approval for formation of a subsidiary for certain business (Section 19); notification of accounts and balance sheet (Section 29); directions for inspection (Section 35); powers to acquire undertakings of banks (Section 36AE); and appointment of a court liquidator attached to the High Court under Section 38A. The Central Government has substantial control over the management of public sector banks (50 per cent or more of the shares of State Bank of India, nationalised banks and regional rural banks are held by the Central Government); only certain provisions of the Banking Regulation Act apply to these banks as indicated in that Act.

Regulation by other authorities (courseware): a banking company is subject to the control of other regulatory agencies in the conduct of its business: under the Companies Act in respect of company matters; to labour authorities in respect of service terms of workmen, opening and closing of premises and engagement of contract labour; to income tax and other taxes such as cash transaction tax and goods and services tax. As provided in Section 6 of the Banking Regulation Act, banks may undertake certain non-banking business in addition to the business of banking and are then subject to the control of other agencies: dealings in securities like shares and debentures are subject to regulation by the Securities and Exchange Board of India under the Securities Contract (Regulation) Act, 1956 read with the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992; if a bank wishes to raise capital through public issue it has to comply with SEBI guidelines; insurance business must follow Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority regulations, and mutual fund and merchant banking business follow Reserve Bank and SEBI rules.

facts.statement: Licence (courseware): to commence or carry on banking business in India a company needs a licence from the Reserve Bank under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; carrying on banking business without a licence is prohibited. Companies existing in 1949 had to apply for a licence within six months of commencement of the Act and could continue until their application was rejected. The requirement ensures only banks established and operating on sound lines continue. The Reserve Bank has discretion to grant or refuse a licence and may impose conditions; a court intervenes only where the decision was made on extraneous or unreasonable grounds (Gujarat High Court, Shivabhai v RBI). In considering an application the Reserve Bank may consider defects revealed in an inspection under Section 35 and a refusal does not stop the company from carrying on other business. Under Section 22(3) the Reserve Bank must be satisfied, by inspection of books or otherwise, that: the company can pay its present and future depositors in full as claims accrue; its affairs are not conducted in a manner detrimental to depositors; the general character of the proposed management is not prejudicial to the public interest or depositors; the company has adequate capital structure and earning prospects; the public interest will be served by the grant; having regard to banking facilities in the proposed area and the potential for expansion, the grant would not prejudice the operation and consolidation of the banking system consistent with monetary stability and economic growth; and any other condition necessary to ensure the business is not prejudicial to the public interest or depositors. The Reserve Bank may stipulate a higher capital than the minimum under Section 11 before granting a licence, being satisfied of adequate capital structure and earning prospects.

Foreign banks, on-tap licensing and cancellation (courseware): a foreign bank applying for a licence to set up wholly owned subsidiaries or branches in India must satisfy the Reserve Bank that it is subject to adequate prudential supervision in its home country, having regard to Basel standards; the setting up of a wholly owned subsidiary or branch should have the approval of the home country regulator; other factors include economic and political relations between India and the country of incorporation, financial soundness of the foreign bank, ownership pattern, ranking and rating, international presence, and that the laws of the home country do not discriminate against banking companies registered in India. Licensing policy for universal banks: after the Finance Minister announced in the 2010-11 budget speech the need to extend geographic coverage, the Reserve Bank issued guidelines for licensing new banks in February 2013 and granted in-principle approval to two new banks; the discussion paper Banking Structure in India of 27 August 2013 favoured continuous authorisation; guidelines for on tap licensing of universal banks in the private sector were published on 1 August 2016, covering eligibility of promoters, fit and proper criteria, corporate structure including non-operative financial holding company, shareholding, minimum voting equity capital, foreign shareholding, governance, business plan and conditions for NBFCs converted into a bank. Small finance banks: first guidelines in 2014; on tap licensing announced in June 2019 and final guidelines issued on 5 December 2019; a small finance bank is registered as a public limited company under the Companies Act, 2013, licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, governed also by the RBI Act, FEMA, the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, the Credit Information Companies Act and the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, and is given scheduled bank status once it commences operations. Cancellation (Section 22(4)): the Reserve Bank may cancel a licence if the company ceases to carry on banking business in India or fails to comply with a condition imposed under sub-section (1) or conditions in sub-sections (3) and (3A); before cancelling for non-compliance it must, unless it considers the delay prejudicial to depositors or the public, give the company an opportunity to take steps to comply. The bank may appeal to the Central Government within thirty days of the date the decision is communicated; the Central Government decision, or the Reserve Bank decision where no appeal is made, is final (Section 22(5) and (6)).

Branches (courseware): under Section 23 a banking company needs the prior permission of the Reserve Bank to open a new place of business in India or abroad, or to change the location of an existing place of business, other than within the same city, town or village; no permission is needed for a temporary place of business not exceeding one month within a city, town or village or its environs where the bank already has a place of business, for providing banking facilities on the occasion of an exhibition, conference or mela or like occasion. Before granting permission the Reserve Bank may require itself to be satisfied by inspection about financial condition and history, the general character of management, adequacy of capital structure and earning prospects and that public interest will be served; it may impose conditions and may revoke permission after giving a reasonable opportunity if conditions are not complied with. Under Section 23(5) place of business includes any sub-office, pay office, sub-pay office or any place at which deposits are received, cheques cashed or moneys lent. For Regional Rural Banks the licence is also given by the Reserve Bank but applications for permission are routed through the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (Section 23, sub-section 4a).

Paid-up capital and reserves (courseware): Section 11 of the Banking Regulation Act sets minimum paid-up capital and reserves for any company wishing to begin banking business; place of business for this purpose means any office, sub-office, pay office, sub-pay office and any place at which deposits are received, cheques cashed or moneys lent; in a dispute about computation the decision of the Reserve Bank is final. A foreign bank incorporated outside India must deposit and keep deposited with the Reserve Bank a prescribed amount in cash or unencumbered approved securities (a larger amount if it has a place of business in Mumbai or Kolkata), and in addition twenty per cent of the profit for each year in respect of business transacted through Indian branches, which may be in approved securities; the Central Government may exempt a foreign bank from the requirement on the Reserve Bank recommendation, and the deposits on cessation of business become assets of the company on which creditors in India have a first charge. For Indian banks Section 11(3) fixes minimum paid-up capital and reserves on a scale depending on the number of States and places of business and whether Mumbai or Kolkata is included, with provisos that for companies commencing business after the 1962 amendment paid-up capital shall not be less than five lakh rupees; the courseware also notes that the Reserve Bank has stipulated specific different minimum capital norms for small finance banks and universal banks in their licensing policy. Capital structure (Section 12(1)): subscribed capital shall not be less than half of authorised capital, and paid-up capital not less than half of subscribed capital; if capital is increased this must be complied with within two years as the Reserve Bank allows. Under the Act, banking companies may issue equity shares or equity and preference shares (perpetual or irredeemable or redeemable) in accordance with Reserve Bank guidelines.

Shareholding (courseware): there is no specified ceiling on a person holding shares in a banking company except the five per cent cap on prior approval under Section 12B and other law; Section 12(2) restricts voting rights: no person holding shares shall exercise voting rights on a poll in excess of ten per cent of the total voting rights of all shareholders; the Reserve Bank may increase this ceiling in a phased manner up to twenty-six per cent. Section 12(3): no suit or proceeding shall be maintained against a registered shareholder on the ground that title to shares vests in another, except a suit by a transferee on a transfer in accordance with law or on behalf of a minor or lunatic. Section 12B: prior approval of the Reserve Bank is mandatory for any person who intends to acquire or agree to acquire, directly or indirectly, shares or voting rights of a banking company which, together with those already held, would entitle the person to five per cent or more of the paid-up share capital or voting rights; transfers of shares are also governed by the Companies Act, 2013; where a bank receives a transfer request taking a party above five per cent it must refer it to the Reserve Bank, which may order the transferee not to exercise voting rights. The aim is that control of banks rests with fit and proper persons. Reports: particulars of shareholding of the Chairman, Managing Director or Chief Executive Officer must be submitted to the Reserve Bank; the Reserve Bank may also order any other information. Section 13 (as amended in 2013): commission, brokerage, discount or remuneration on the sale of shares of a banking company shall not exceed two and a half per cent of the price at which the shares are issued (earlier linked to the paid-up value). Dividend: the courseware states earlier Reserve Bank conditions for declaring a dividend (profit of the current year, minimum capital adequacy and net NPA tests, the bank must comply with Sections 15 and 17, and a payout ratio normally not above 40 per cent). Section 15 prohibits payment of dividend until all capitalised expenses are written off and Section 17 requires transfer of a specified portion of profit to the statutory reserve fund.

Subsidiaries and other companies (courseware): Section 19 restricts the formation of subsidiaries to prevent banks from carrying on trading activities by acquiring a controlling interest in non-banking companies. A bank may form a subsidiary only for: any business permissible to banking companies under Section 6(1) clauses (a) to (o); carrying on the business of banking exclusively outside India (with the Reserve Bank prior permission); and any other business which the Reserve Bank, with the prior approval of the Central Government, considers conducive to the spread of banking in India or otherwise useful or necessary in the public interest. Business undertaken by a subsidiary is not treated as the bank itself taking up that business for Section 8. Under Section 19(2) a bank cannot hold shares in any company as pledgee, mortgagee or absolute owner of an amount exceeding thirty per cent of the paid-up share capital of that company or thirty per cent of its own paid-up share capital and reserves, whichever is less; shares in any company in which its managing director or manager is interested are prohibited except for a subsidiary; a bank may form a subsidiary for credit information business. Section 29A allows the Reserve Bank to order inspection of associate enterprises (holding company, subsidiary, joint venture, or companies exercising control over board composition or significant influence over financial or policy decisions) with Section 35 inspection provisions applying.

Board of directors (courseware): Section 10A requires that at least fifty-one per cent of the total number of directors be persons with special knowledge or practical experience in accountancy, agriculture and rural economy, banking, co-operation, economics, finance, law, small scale industry or any other matter the Reserve Bank considers useful; at least two of the directors must have special knowledge in agriculture and rural economy or co-operation or small scale industry. Substantial interest: a director shall not have substantial interest in a company or firm carrying on trade, commerce or industry as an employee, manager or managing agent (Section 10A(2)(b)); companies under Section 25 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 8 of the 2013 Act) and small scale industrial concerns are excluded and proprietors of trading, commercial or industrial concerns other than small scale industrial concerns are also disqualified. Substantial interest is defined in Section 5(ne) by beneficial holding by an individual or spouse or minor child exceeding a fixed sum or ten per cent of the paid-up capital, and in firms by a share exceeding ten per cent of total capital. Period of office: directors other than the chairman or a whole-time director shall not hold office for more than eight years continuously (a removed chairman or whole-time director ceases to be director and is not eligible for further appointment as director for four years). Reconstitution: where a board is not constituted per Section 10A, the Reserve Bank can order reconstitution, if necessary by retirement of directors by lots, and if the bank does not comply within two months the Reserve Bank may remove any director and appoint a new one, whose term would be what the predecessor would have held; no proceedings of a banking company are invalid only because of a defect in the composition of the board.

Chairman and managing director (courseware): Section 10B requires every banking company to have a whole-time or part-time chairman appointed from among its directors; a whole-time chairman manages the entire affairs; a part-time chairman requires prior Reserve Bank approval, and in the absence of a chairman the whole affairs are entrusted to a managing director, subject to superintendence, control and directions of the board. A whole-time chairman and a managing director hold office for not more than five years as the board fixes and are eligible for re-election or reappointment; the whole-time chairman or managing director may continue after the term until the successor assumes office, with Reserve Bank approval. Qualifications (Section 10B(4)): special knowledge and practical experience of the working of a banking company, the State Bank of India or a subsidiary bank or a financial institution, or of financial, economic or business administration; a person is disqualified from a whole-time chairman or managing director post if he or she is a director of any company other than a subsidiary of the bank or a Section 25 company, a partner of a firm carrying on trade, business or industry, has substantial interest in any other company or firm, is a director, manager, managing agent, partner or proprietor of any trading, commercial or industrial concern, or is engaged in any other business or vocation. Removal: if the Reserve Bank thinks the person is not fit and proper it may require the banking company to remove the person and appoint a suitable person, after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard; failing compliance within two months the Reserve Bank may remove and appoint; appeal lies to the Central Government within thirty days and the Government order, or the Reserve Bank order if no appeal is filed, is final and not challengeable in any civil court. Temporary arrangements for a vacancy caused by death, resignation or incapacity may be made for a period not exceeding four months with Reserve Bank approval. Section 10BB: where the office of chairman or managing director falls vacant and is not filled, the Reserve Bank may appoint a person for a period not exceeding three years, who may be reappointed once and removed by the Reserve Bank, with allowances determined by it. Section 10C exempts the whole-time chairman or managing director from holding qualification shares, and Section 10A directors have a similar exemption. Sections 10A, 10B and 10BB override other laws and contracts and no one affected by action under them has a claim to compensation for loss of office. The Financial Services Institutions Bureau, constituted from 1 July 2022, recommends persons for appointment as whole-time directors and non-executive chairpersons on the boards of financial services institutions and replaces the earlier Banks Board Bureau.

Additional directors, restrictions and Reserve Bank control (courseware): Section 36AB lets the Reserve Bank appoint additional directors to a bank board if in the interest of banking policy, the public or the bank and its depositors it is necessary; such directors hold office at the pleasure of the Reserve Bank for a period not exceeding three years, and further periods not exceeding three years at a time; they incur no liability for acts in good faith, need not hold qualification shares, and are not counted for working out proportions of directors required by the Act. Section 10 restricts employment: a bank shall not employ or continue a managing agent or an employee who is or has been adjudicated insolvent, or suspended payment or compounded with creditors; who has been convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude; whose remuneration is by way of commission or share in profits; or whose remuneration the Reserve Bank considers excessive (the restriction applies to workmen as management personnel per Central Bank of India v Their Workmen, but does not affect bonus under a settlement, or commission paid to brokers or agents who are not regular staff). Persons who are directors of companies other than a subsidiary or a Section 25 / Section 8 company are prohibited from managing a banking company, subject to temporary relaxation allowed by the Reserve Bank. Section 36AA empowers the Reserve Bank to remove any chairman, director, chief executive officer or other officer or employee of a banking company in the public interest, to prevent affairs being conducted detrimentally to depositors, or to secure proper management; before the order the person must have a reasonable opportunity of making a representation, but where urgency demands, the Reserve Bank may bar the person from acting pending consideration. Appeal lies to the Central Government within thirty days of communication, and its decision is final. The removed person ceases to hold office, is prohibited from taking part directly or indirectly in the management of the bank for a period of up to five years as specified, and is punishable for contravention with a fine of Rs 250 for each day of contravention. The Reserve Bank may appoint a suitable person in place for a period not exceeding three years, extendable by further periods of up to three years, who incurs no liability for good faith actions. Section 36ACA allows the Reserve Bank to supersede the board of a banking company for six months, extendable up to twelve months; an Administrator is appointed assisted by a committee of three or more persons and vacates office when the board is reconstituted.

Corporate governance (courseware): the OECD describes the purpose of corporate governance as helping to build an environment of trust, transparency and accountability for long-term investment, financial stability and business integrity. The first major study in India: the Cadbury Committee (UK, 1992); the OECD principles were first published in 1999 and revised in 2004. The six OECD principles (2004): ensuring the basis for an effective corporate governance framework; the rights of shareholders and key ownership functions; the equitable treatment of shareholders (including minority and foreign shareholders); the role of stakeholders; disclosure and transparency; and the responsibilities of the board. Banks hold a special position because they accept and deploy large amounts of public funds in fiduciary capacity and are key to the payment system. The Basel Committee guidance on enhancing corporate governance for banking organisations (February 2006) highlights the roles of boards and senior management (with independent directors), management of conflicts of interest, internal and external auditors and internal control, transparency, and the role of supervisors. In India the Reserve Bank, SEBI and the Department of Company Affairs are concerned. Committees: Dr A.S. Ganguly (Consultative Group, set up in November 2001, report in 2002), Dr R.H. Patil (advisory group on corporate governance, March 2001) and Shri M.S. Verma (advisory group on banking supervision, January 2003). The Reserve Bank introduced the concept of fit and proper criteria for directors (collecting information, due diligence, a nomination committee of the board to scrutinise the declarations). Directors: the board should ensure the responsibilities of directors are well defined and private sector banks should have directors representing specific sectors as provided under the Act; as a matter of desirable practice not more than one member of a family or close relative should be on the board of a bank; the chief executive officer must satisfy the fit and proper criteria; the Reserve Bank may apply additional criteria for the chairman and chief executive. For public sector banks corporate governance principles were statutorily recognised through the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) and Financial Institutions Laws (Amendment) Act, 2006, which require shareholder directors to be fit and proper persons (Section 9(2)), the Reserve Bank notifying the criteria.

facts.statement: Power to issue directions (courseware): the Reserve Bank may issue directions to banks under Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; those directions are binding on the bank or banks to which they are addressed even if not expressly described as statutory instructions. Section 21 gives power to regulate advances; Section 35A gives wide powers generally; the Reserve Bank has been issuing directions on rates of interest and other terms of acceptance of deposits and the making of loans and advances under Section 21 read with Section 35A. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2017 inserted Sections 35AA and 35AB empowering the Reserve Bank to intervene directly in settling bad loan cases. Case law cited: the Gujarat High Court held that a Master Circular on wilful defaulters issued under statutory powers has the force of law even though it does not refer to a statute, and is not an impermissible delegation of legislative power; a non-statutory circular cannot create legal rights (State Bank of India v CIT); directions bind banks and not customers or the public; directions operate prospectively and a violation does not invalidate contracts with third parties (BOI Finance v Custodian); the power must be exercised in good faith (the supersession of a co-operative bank board upheld in the Harisidh co-operative bank case). Section 36(1)(a) allows the Reserve Bank to caution or prohibit banking companies against entering into any particular transaction or class of transactions and generally to give advice.

Acceptance of deposits (courseware): banks accept time and demand deposits from the public (fixed and recurring deposits are repayable after an agreed period, current and savings accounts are repayable on demand), subject to the terms and conditions agreed with the depositor and to Reserve Bank directions. Section 35A(c) lets the Reserve Bank give directions on acceptance of deposits in public interest, banking policy or depositor interest; at present the Reserve Bank prescribes only certain moratoria on acceptance of deposits, minimum and maximum period of deposits and the interest rates on NRI deposits, and clarifications on bulk deposits and KYC. Deposit insurance: deposits of banks including Regional Rural Banks and co-operative banks come within the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act as amended in 2021, under which the bank pays an account holder up to the insured amount within 90 days if a bank comes under a moratorium. Returns on unclaimed deposits (Section 26): a bank must file a return every year within thirty days of the end of the calendar year of all deposits not operated for ten years (for fixed deposits, ten years from the expiry of the period of the deposit). The Banking Laws amendment of 2013 inserted Section 26A creating the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund to take over deposits not claimed or operated for ten years or more, within three months from the expiry of the ten years; the amount can be claimed back by the depositor or legal heirs or nominees at any time. Eligible accounts include savings, fixed or term deposits, cumulative or recurring deposits, current accounts, cash credit accounts, and balances of drafts, pay orders, bankers cheques and similar instruments.

Nomination (courseware): Section 45ZA of the Banking Regulation Act empowers a depositor or depositors of a banking company (which includes a co-operative bank) to nominate one person as nominee, in the prescribed manner, to whom the amount of the deposit will be returned on the death of the sole depositor or all depositors. The nominee must be the person entitled to all the rights of the depositor in the amount; the nomination can be varied or cancelled at any time by the depositor. Where the nominee is a minor, a person may be appointed to receive the amount on behalf of the minor. Payment to a nominee gives the bank a valid discharge, but does not affect the right of any claimant (such as a legal heir) against the nominee in respect of the amount received. Courts have held (Ram Chander Talwar v Devender Kumar Talwar) that nomination only ensures protection of the estate of the deceased until legal representatives take appropriate steps for succession. Rule 2 of the Banking Companies (Nomination) Rules, 1985 provides the procedure and forms for deposits; the Co-operative Banks (Nomination) Rules, 1985 provide similar rules. Articles in safe custody and safe deposit lockers: Sections 45ZC and 45ZE allow nomination of one person to receive the articles in the event of the death of the person who leaves articles in safe custody or hires a locker; the bank gets a valid discharge on return of the articles to the nominee, after an inventory in the prescribed manner for lockers. Banks must establish the identity of survivor or nominee and the fact of death with documentary evidence, find out whether any order from courts or forums restrains the bank from giving access, and make it clear that access is given only as a trustee of the legal heirs of the deceased hirer so that it does not affect the right or claim any person may have against the survivor or nominee. In a joint locker with survivorship clause, the mandate of the hirers is followed; similar procedure applies to articles in safe custody.

Loans and advances (courseware): lending is a core business of banks. Section 21 empowers the Reserve Bank to issue directions to control advances by banking companies generally or to any particular company, when satisfied that it is necessary in public interest, in the interests of depositors or in the interests of banking policy. Directions may cover: the purpose for which advances may or may not be made; margins to be maintained for secured advances; the maximum amount of advances or financial accommodation to any company, firm, association of persons or individuals, having regard to paid-up capital, reserves and deposits; the maximum amount of guarantees; and the rate of interest and other terms and conditions of advances. Selective credit control: the Reserve Bank may impose measures to prevent speculative hoarding of essential commodities (food grains, pulses, edible oils, sugar, jaggery, cotton and textiles) by regulating the quantum of credit and the rate at which it is extended; such measures have been little used in recent years. Restrictions on loans and advances (Section 20): a banking company cannot grant loans on the security of its own shares, and cannot enter into any commitment for granting loans or advances to or on behalf of any of its directors, or to firms in which any director is interested as partner, manager, employee or guarantor, or any company (other than a Section 25 / Section 8 company) in which a director holds substantial interest or is a director, managing agent, manager, employee or guarantor; loans to an individual whose guarantor or partner is a director are also barred. Where a transaction is doubtful as a loan or advance, the decision of the Reserve Bank is final. Section 20A: a banking company needs prior permission of the Reserve Bank to remit any debt to its directors or to a firm or company in which a director is interested; remission in contravention is void and of no effect.

Regulation of interest rates (courseware): the Reserve Bank regulates interest rates under Section 21 read with Section 35A. In regulating, there should be no discrimination against any class of depositors or loanees without justification in law (Harjit Singh v Union of India). Deposit interest rates were not regulated until 1964; later the Reserve Bank gave directions fixing deposit rates; interest rates on deposits and loans have been deregulated, subject to directions; savings deposit rates are regulated within the terms of the Reserve Bank Directions of 2016 as updated. Lending rates: advances interest is regulated under Section 21(2)(e) of the Act, but banks have freedom to decide lending rates, subject to directions on interest rates for weaker sections, exporters and small loans. The BPLR system (2003) was replaced by the Base Rate (1 July 2010), then the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) from 1 April 2016 (comprising the marginal cost of funds, negative carry on account of CRR, operating costs and a tenor premium). The courseware then states that from 1 October 2019 all new floating rate personal or retail loans and floating rate loans to micro and small enterprises (and from 1 April 2020 to medium enterprises) must be linked to an external benchmark: the Reserve Bank repo rate, the three month or six month Treasury Bill yield published by the Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd, or any other benchmark market interest rate published by it. Banks are free to choose the spread; credit risk premium may change only on a substantial change in the borrower credit assessment; the interest rate under an external benchmark shall be reset at least once in three months; the same bank may not adopt multiple benchmarks within a loan category. Usurious Loans Act, 1918 and Section 21A of the Banking Regulation Act: Section 21A provides that a transaction between a banking company and its debtor cannot be reopened by any court on the ground that the rate of interest charged is excessive; this overrides the Usurious Loans Act and other debt relief laws.

Internet banking (courseware): the Reserve Bank set up a Working Group on Internet banking that focused on technology and security, legal, and regulatory and supervisory issues. Highlights: banks should have a security policy approved by the Board; logical access controls (user ids, passwords, smart cards, biometrics); public key infrastructure should be the favoured technology; periodic penetration tests; physical access controls; backed-up data tested for recovery; disaster recovery sites; legal issues: accounts opened over the internet only after proper physical verification of identity; the Consumer Protection Act applies to banking services; regulatory issues: prior approval of the Reserve Bank for providing internet banking, reporting of breaches, only members of the cheque clearing system to participate in inter-bank payment gateways. The courseware adds that a November 2015 circular lays down the framework for internet banking facility for co-operative banks (view-only facility and transactional facility with prior approval and eligibility tests); general guidelines of 14 June 2001 and 5 November 2015 are referred to.

Money market instruments (courseware): the Reserve Bank of India (Amendment) Act, 2006 (Section 45W) empowers the Reserve Bank in public interest to regulate the financial system, to determine policy relating to interest rates or interest rate products and give directions to any agencies dealing in securities, money market instruments, foreign exchange, derivatives or instruments of like nature; the directions do not relate to the execution or settlement of trades on recognised stock exchanges. Call, notice and term money market: participants permitted include scheduled commercial banks (excluding local area banks), payment banks, small finance banks, regional rural banks, co-operative banks and primary dealers; prudential limits on borrowing are set as a percentage of capital funds or aggregate deposits (details dated and not taught). Certificates of deposit are issued by scheduled commercial banks, regional rural banks and small finance banks, in dematerialised form, held with a depository registered with SEBI, with a minimum denomination and tenor of seven days to one year, issued on a T+1 basis; banks may not grant loans against CDs; buyback only after a period. Commercial paper is a money market instrument under Section 45W issued under the Reserve Bank Commercial Paper Directions of 10 August 2017; eligible issuers include corporates, non-banking financial companies and all-India financial institutions meeting conditions; CP is issued in dematerialised form, as a promissory note at a discount to face value, with minimum credit rating A3, no underwriting or co-acceptance, and no options (call or put).

Banking Ombudsman and the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (courseware): an Ombudsman is an independent non-partisan authority appointed to investigate public grievances and redress them as a non-adversarial alternative to courts. The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 1995 was framed by the Reserve Bank under Section 35A, modified in 2002 and replaced by the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006. The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 integrates the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006, the Ombudsman Scheme for Non-Banking Financial Companies, 2018 and the Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions, 2019, which were repealed; it is framed under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, Section 45L of the RBI Act and Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act and is focused on cost-free redress of complaints involving deficiency in service by regulated entities if not resolved to the satisfaction of the customer or not replied within 30 days by the regulated entity. Salient features: it is not necessary for a complainant to identify under which scheme to complain; deficiency in service is the ground, with a list of excluded grounds; the Scheme has done away with the jurisdiction of each ombudsman office; a Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre at the Reserve Bank in Chandigarh receives and processes complaints; the Principal Nodal Officer of the regulated entity, not below the rank of General Manager or equivalent, represents it; the regulated entity cannot appeal against an award if it did not furnish information in time; the Executive Director in charge of Consumer Education and Protection Department of the Reserve Bank is the Appellate Authority. The ombudsman must comply with Reserve Bank directions; the Scheme cannot override debt recovery tribunal jurisdiction, and where a complaint is under consideration by a court, tribunal or arbitrator the ombudsman cannot proceed (Durga Hotel Complex v Reserve Bank).

Financial stability and the reserve fund (courseware): financial stability has been defined by the Reserve Bank in its first Financial Stability Report (March 2010) as a situation in which the financial sector provides critical services to the real economy without discontinuity. Provisions in the Banking Regulation Act and the Reserve Bank Act promote stability through regulation of banks: reserve funds, cash reserve, statutory liquidity ratio and assets in India. Reserve fund (Section 17(1) of the Banking Regulation Act): every banking company incorporated in India must create a reserve fund; every year a sum equal to not less than twenty per cent of the profits as shown in the profit and loss account must be transferred to the reserve fund before any dividend is declared. The Reserve Bank instructed (circular of 23 September 2000) that commercial banks other than foreign banks must transfer not less than 25 per cent of net profit after tax from the year ending 31 March 2001, as stated in the courseware. Exemption: if a bank has adequate paid-up capital and reserves in relation to its deposit liabilities, the Reserve Bank may recommend to the Central Government exemption; no exemption is made unless the reserve fund together with the share premium account is not less than the paid-up capital. Appropriation from the reserve fund or share premium account must be reported to the Reserve Bank within twenty-one days. Foreign banks keep a deposit with the Reserve Bank of twenty per cent of annual profits of Indian business instead (Section 11(2)). Section 29A inserted by the 2013 amendment lets the Reserve Bank direct a bank to furnish statements and information on its business and affairs of associate enterprises.

Cash reserve (courseware): every scheduled bank has to maintain a cash reserve with the Reserve Bank under Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act; in the case of non-scheduled banks, Section 18 of the Banking Regulation Act provides for the cash reserve. A scheduled bank is a bank included in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank Act; under Section 42(6) the Reserve Bank may include a bank if it has paid-up capital and reserves of an aggregate value of not less than Rs 5 lakh, satisfies the Reserve Bank that its affairs are not conducted detrimental to depositors, and is a State co-operative bank, a company as defined in Section 3 of the Companies Act, an institution notified by the Central Government, or a corporation or a company incorporated outside India (foreign bank). The Reserve Bank may exclude a bank if its paid-up capital and reserves fall below the limit or its affairs are conducted detrimentally to depositors or it goes into liquidation. Quantum (Section 42(1)): an average daily balance, as amended in 2006, of such per cent of the total of demand and time liabilities in India as the Reserve Bank notifies from time to time, having regard to the needs of securing monetary stability; the Reserve Bank can fix the ratio without any ceiling or floor rate (earlier floor three per cent and ceiling twenty per cent). Average daily balance is the average of the balances held at the close of business each day for the fortnight; the liabilities exclude paid-up capital, reserves and credit balance in the profit and loss account. Scheduled banks must maintain a minimum CRR balance of up to ninety per cent of the average daily required reserve on all days during the fortnight (courseware states 90 per cent). No interest is payable on CRR balances since the 2006 amendment. Returns: every scheduled bank submits a return, signed by two responsible officers, within seven days of the close of business on every alternate Friday, to the Reserve Bank (Section 42(2)); the Reserve Bank can allow provisional returns within seven days followed by final returns. Penalties: if the balance falls below the stipulated minimum, the bank is liable to penal interest at three per cent above the bank rate for the first fortnight and five per cent above the bank rate if the shortfall continues in the next fortnight; if the shortfall continues in the third fortnight each director, manager or secretary knowingly and wilfully party to the default is punishable with a fine; the Reserve Bank can also prohibit the bank from accepting fresh deposits. Penalty is payable within fourteen days of demand and the Reserve Bank may recover it as a decree of a civil court. Non-scheduled banks keep not less than three per cent of demand and time liabilities as at the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight, either in cash or as balance in current account with the Reserve Bank, and submit a monthly return by the twentieth day of the month.

Statutory liquidity ratio and assets in India (courseware): every banking company has to maintain a certain percentage of its net demand and time liabilities as liquid assets in India under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, in the form and manner notified by the Reserve Bank. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Ordinance, 2007 amended Section 24, removing the statutory floor of 25 per cent; under Section 24(2A) the scheduled bank in addition to the average daily balance of Section 42 of the RBI Act maintains assets valued at not less than such percentage as the Reserve Bank notifies, not exceeding 40 per cent of its total net demand and time liabilities on the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight. Non-scheduled banks maintain SLR assets in addition to the cash reserve under Section 18. Returns: a monthly return is submitted within twenty days after the month end showing the assets and liabilities at the close of business on every alternate Friday. Penalty for default: penal interest at three per cent above the bank rate on the shortfall, rising to five per cent above the bank rate if the default continues on the succeeding alternate Friday; directors, managers and secretaries of the bank are punishable with a fine on continued default; the Reserve Bank may waive the penalty when it is satisfied that the bank had sufficient reason. Assets in India (Section 25): the assets in India of every banking company at the close of business on the last Friday of every quarter shall not be less than 75 per cent of its demand and time liabilities in India; the bank submits a return within one month from the end of every quarter; regional rural banks submit the report to NABARD. Assets include cash, gold or unencumbered approved securities, and export bills drawn in India and import bills drawn on and payable in India approved by the Reserve Bank; paid-up capital, reserves and credit balance in the profit and loss account are not liabilities in India for this purpose.
