facts.statement: Annual accounts and balance sheet (courseware): Section 29 of the Banking Regulation Act requires every banking company to prepare its balance sheet and profit and loss account as at the end of each calendar year, or on the expiry of the twelve months ending with any other date the Central Government notifies; foreign banks cover the business transacted through all their branches in India. In preparing accounts banks comply with Reserve Bank directions on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning. The accounts of a banking company incorporated in India are signed by the manager or principal officer and at least three directors (or all if not more than three directors); for foreign banks, by the manager or agent at the principal office in India. The forms are in the Third Schedule, and the Central Government may amend the form after not less than three months notice. The Companies Act 2013 provision on true and fair view and Schedule III formats does not apply to banking companies as the Banking Regulation Act has overriding effect (Section 29(3A) makes certain Companies Act provisions on the profit and loss account period inapplicable). Listed banks publish unaudited quarterly results (clause 41 of the listing agreement as cited). Publication (Section 31 with Rule 15 of the Banking Regulation (Companies) Rules, 1949): the accounts and balance sheet with the auditors report are published in a newspaper circulated at the place of the principal office within six months from the end of the period; newspaper means one published at least once a week but not a journal other than a newspaper. Submission: three copies of the balance sheet, profit and loss account and auditors report to the Reserve Bank within three months of the end of the period, extendable by up to a further three months. For the Registrar of Companies, Section 32 of the Banking Regulation Act requires three copies to the Registrar, dealt with as if submitted under the Companies Act.

Audit and auditors (courseware): Section 30(1) of the Banking Regulation Act requires the balance sheet and profit and loss account prepared under Section 29 to be audited by a person duly qualified under any law for the time being in force to be an auditor of companies. Section 30(1A) requires Reserve Bank approval for the appointment, reappointment or removal of auditors of a banking company. The auditor has the powers, functions and duties of a company auditor and the liabilities and penalties (Section 227 of the Companies Act 1956, Section 143 of the 2013 Act) and in the audit report of a bank incorporated in India must state: whether information and explanations required were found satisfactory; whether transactions are within the powers of the company; whether returns from branches were adequate; whether the profit and loss account shows a true picture of profit or loss; and any other matter the auditor considers necessary to bring to the notice of the shareholders. The auditor of a bank is not restricted to safeguarding promoters but also owes responsibility to depositors, the public and other stakeholders because the bank deals with public money; an auditor can be blamed if after an apparently sound balance sheet is certified the bank is found insolvent (cases cited). The Reserve Bank in 2018 put in place an Enforcement Action Framework in respect of lapses of statutory auditors of commercial banks to ensure quality audits. Special audit (Section 30(1B)): the Reserve Bank may order a special audit of the accounts of any banking company in the public interest or in the interest of the banking company or its depositors, relating to any transaction or class of transactions or any period; the audit may be by the same or a different qualified auditor appointed by the Reserve Bank or by the statutory auditor; the order binds the bank and auditor; the auditor reports to the Reserve Bank with a copy to the bank; and the bank bears the expenses.

Returns (courseware): a banking company submits returns of several kinds. Section 24(3): a return of liquid assets within twenty days of the end of the month, in the form prescribed by Rule 13A of the Banking Regulation (Companies) Rules, 1949, giving assets and demand and time liabilities at the close of business on each alternate Friday; the Reserve Bank may also require a return of assets and liabilities as at each day of the month. Section 27 (monthly returns): each month a return showing assets and liabilities as at the close of business on the last Friday of the previous month, submitted before the close of the following month in the form prescribed by Rule 14A; the Reserve Bank may call for statements and information on business and affairs at any time and may also seek half-yearly returns on investments or classification of advances by industry, commerce or agriculture. Annual accounts and balance sheet: submitted to the Reserve Bank within three months, extendable by a further three months. Section 25(1): a quarterly return on assets in India within one month of the quarter end, in Rule 14A form. Section 26: a return of unclaimed deposits within thirty days of the end of each calendar year, in the form of Rule 14B. Non-scheduled banks: cash reserve return under Section 18 by the twentieth of the month, with the form in Rule 13A. Scheduled banks: returns under Section 42 of the Reserve Bank Act in Form I. A defaulting bank is liable to penal interest at 3 per cent above the bank rate on the shortfall in the cash reserve and 5 per cent above for each subsequent day if the default continues.

Preservation of records and paid instruments (courseware): Section 45Y of the Banking Regulation Act lets the Central Government, after consulting the Reserve Bank, make rules specifying the periods for which a banking company shall preserve its books, accounts and other documents, and shall preserve and keep with itself different instruments paid by it. The rules are the Banking Companies (Period of Preservation of Records) Rules, 1985 and the Co-operative Banks (Period of Preservation of Books) Rules, 1985, which specify different periods for different ledgers and registers; the Reserve Bank in January 2008, relying on the Central Information Commission legal view on the Right to Information Act, advised that banks may follow the existing rules; the Reserve Bank may direct a longer period under Section 35A. Under the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, banks maintain a record of: all cash transactions of more than Rs 10 lakh or equivalent in foreign currency; a series of connected cash transactions below Rs 10 lakh within a month whose aggregate exceeds Rs 10 lakh; all receipts by non-profit organisations of more than Rs 10 lakh; all transactions where forged or counterfeit currency notes have been used; and all suspicious transactions. Records should allow reconstruction of individual transactions and include the nature of the transaction, the amount and currency, the date and the parties. Banks must keep records of transactions, domestic and foreign, for at least five years from the date of the transaction between the bank and the client, and identification documents for at least five years after the business relationship has ended. Return of paid instruments (Section 45Z): a bank may return paid instruments to customers even before the end of the preservation period, but must not return an instrument without making and keeping a true copy by mechanical or other process; the bank may recover from the customer the cost of making copies; customer includes a Government department and a corporation incorporated by or under any law.

Inspection, scrutiny and government-ordered inspection (courseware): under Section 35(1) the Reserve Bank may at any time inspect any banking company and its books and accounts. The Reserve Bank conducts the Annual Financial Inspection of banking companies; now this consists mainly of assessing all types of risks under risk based supervision through the Supervisory Program for Assessment of Risk and Capital (SPARC), ending with Risk Assessment Reports. The Reserve Bank may also conduct any other inspection, including of bank branches, at any time, and must inspect in compliance with a direction of the Central Government, giving the Central Government a copy of the report; after an inspection the bank is given a copy of the inspection report. During inspection officials of the banking company including directors must produce all books, accounts and documents in their custody and the inspecting officer may examine any director or officer on oath. Inspection at the behest of the Government: a copy of the report is sent to the Government, which may after giving the bank an opportunity to make a representation prohibit it from receiving fresh deposits, cancel or modify an order subject to terms, and may publish the inspection report or any part of it if it thinks fit. Scrutiny (Section 35(1A)): the Reserve Bank may at any time cause a scrutiny of the affairs of a banking company and its books and accounts by officers; unlike inspection, providing a copy of the scrutiny report to the bank is not mandatory, but must be provided if the bank asks for it or if adverse action is contemplated; the Reserve Bank may call for books, accounts, documents, statements and information, and may examine on oath any director or officer.

Board for Financial Supervision (courseware): the Reserve Bank inspects and supervises banks; in 1993 the Department of Banking Supervision was set up and in November 1994 the Board for Financial Supervision (BFS) was set up under Regulation 4 of the Reserve Bank of India (Board for Financial Supervision) Regulations, 1994 to provide integrated supervision of credit institutions including commercial and co-operative banks, all-India financial institutions, local area banks, small finance banks, payment banks, credit information companies, non-banking financial companies and primary dealers. The Department of Banking Supervision was bifurcated into the Department of Banking Supervision and the Department of Non-Banking Supervision in August 1997, and later the Department of Co-operative Banking Supervision was set up. From 1 November 2019 the supervision and inspection functions were integrated into a unified Department of Supervision. From 1 April 2019 Section 45NAA of the Reserve Bank Act lets the Reserve Bank direct a non-banking financial company to furnish information relating to its group companies. Composition: the Governor of the Reserve Bank is the chairman; one of the Deputy Governors (usually the one in charge of supervision) nominated by the Governor is the vice chairman; four directors of the Central Board nominated by the Governor for a specified period are members. A sub-committee of the BFS was constituted in April 2018 under Regulations 11 and 12; it exercises the supervision and inspection powers for payments banks, small finance banks, local area banks, small foreign banks, select urban co-operative banks, select non-banking financial companies and credit information companies, and is chaired by the Deputy Governor in charge of supervision. Functions include: fine tuning the supervisory processes; off-site surveillance; strengthening statutory audit and the role of auditors; strengthening internal defences such as corporate governance, internal control and audit and risk control; a supervisory rating system; supervision of overseas operations of Indian banks and consolidated supervision; technical assistance for co-operative banks; a Prompt Corrective Action framework for weak banks; a fraud risk management framework; risk based supervision; an enforcement framework; a credit registry for large borrowers; and a subsidiary for IT requirements including cyber security. Meetings: normally once every month, with three members, of whom one is the chairman or vice chairman, as the quorum. DAKSH, launched on 6 October 2022, is a web-based workflow application for monitoring compliance by supervised entities.

Acquisition of undertakings (courseware): Section 36AE of the Banking Regulation Act lets the Central Government acquire the undertaking of a banking company, which means its entire organisation (R.C. Cooper v Union of India). Conditions: on receipt of a report from the Reserve Bank the Central Government is satisfied that the banking company (a) has on more than one occasion failed to comply with directions given in writing under Section 21 or 35A relating to banking policy, or (b) is being managed in a manner detrimental to the interests of its depositors, in the interests of banking policy or for the better provision of credit. The Government may, after consultation with the Reserve Bank, acquire the undertaking by a notified order from a specified date (the appointed day), after giving the bank a reasonable opportunity of showing cause. On acquisition all assets and liabilities of the acquired bank vest in the Central Government, which may order vesting in a company or corporation (the transferee bank). Section 36AF: the Central Government makes a scheme for the acquired bank in consultation with the Reserve Bank on property, assets, liabilities, board of management, service of employees and payment of compensation to shareholders; the scheme is placed before Parliament, has overriding effect and binds the acquired bank, its members, creditors and depositors. Section 36AG: shareholders of the acquired bank are entitled to compensation determined in accordance with the principles in the Fifth Schedule; Section 36AH provides for reference to a tribunal if the compensation offered is not acceptable; a foreign bank may request a reference.

Amalgamation and moratorium (courseware): Voluntary amalgamation (Section 44A): a banking company may be amalgamated with another; the scheme is placed before the shareholders of both companies, and must be approved by a resolution passed by a majority in number representing two-thirds in value of the shareholders of each company present in person or by proxy; every shareholder gets notice; a shareholder who votes against or dissents and gives notice may claim the value of his shares from the bank in the event the Reserve Bank sanctions the scheme; after approval the scheme is submitted to the Reserve Bank for sanction; on sanction the assets and liabilities pass to the transferee bank and the Reserve Bank may direct that the amalgamated company stands dissolved. Amalgamation by Government: the Central Government may order the amalgamation of two banking companies under Section 396 of the Companies Act 1956 (Section 237 of the 2013 Act), but only after consulting the Reserve Bank. Moratorium (Section 45): where it appears good reason exists, the Reserve Bank may apply to the Central Government for a moratorium, staying the commencement or continuation of any action or proceedings against the bank for a fixed period on such terms as the Government thinks fit; the period is extendable from time to time but the total period shall not exceed six months; during moratorium the bank shall not make any payment to depositors or discharge liabilities unless the Central Government directs. Scheme: during the moratorium or at any time the Reserve Bank may prepare a scheme for the reconstruction of the banking company or its amalgamation with another bank if necessary in the public interest, in the interests of the depositors, for securing proper management or in the interest of the banking system; the scheme may provide for constitution, name and capital of the reconstructed or transferee bank, transfer of assets, change in the board, alteration of the memorandum, reduction of the interest or rights of members, depositors or creditors, payment in cash, allotment of shares and continuation of service of employees. Employees continue on the same terms; within three years of the scheme employees may opt out. Sanction: a copy of the draft scheme goes to the Government and the banks concerned, which may send suggestions within a period fixed by the Reserve Bank; the Government may sanction the scheme with modifications and it comes into force on the date specified. Effect: the sanction by the Government is conclusive evidence of compliance with Section 45; assets and liabilities vest in the transferee bank; difficulties can be removed by order laid before Parliament; the Central Government may give exemptions for not more than seven years; a single scheme may cover several banks under moratorium; the provisions of Section 45 and the scheme have overriding effect over other laws, agreements, awards or instruments.

Winding up of banks (courseware): winding up of a bank is the process of dissolution when it ceases to do business as usual, to sell off assets, pay creditors and distribute any remaining amount to shareholders; the Banking Regulation Act provides a machinery by which winding up proceedings are expedited. Suspension of business (Section 37): a banking company temporarily unable to meet obligations may apply to the High Court for staying the commencement or continuance of proceedings for a fixed period; the total moratorium shall not exceed six months; the application must be supported by a report of the Reserve Bank that the bank will be able to pay its debts if the application is allowed; if the Reserve Bank is satisfied that the bank is being conducted detrimentally to the interests of depositors it may apply to the High Court for winding up. Winding up by the High Court (Section 38): the High Court shall order winding up if the bank is unable to pay its debts or an application has been made by the Reserve Bank under Section 37 or Section 38; the Reserve Bank is bound to apply if directed by the Central Government under Section 35(4) after an inspection or scrutiny at its direction; and the Reserve Bank may apply where the bank fails to comply with Section 11 on minimum paid-up capital and reserves, is not entitled to carry on banking under Section 22 by rejection or cancellation of licence, is prohibited from accepting fresh deposits under Section 35(4) or Section 42(3A) of the Reserve Bank Act, fails to comply with requirements under Section 11 beyond the period specified, or in the opinion of the Reserve Bank a compromise or arrangement cannot be worked, the returns show it cannot pay its debts or its continuance is prejudicial to the interests of the depositors. A bank is deemed unable to pay its debts if it has refused to meet any lawful demand made at any of its offices or branches within the stipulated time and the Reserve Bank certifies in writing that the bank is unable to pay its debts: two days where the Reserve Bank has an office, branch or agency, otherwise five days. In the Palai Central Bank case the Supreme Court held that the decision to wind up in the interests of depositors is reasonably left to the Reserve Bank. Court liquidator (Section 38A): attached to every High Court, appointed by the Central Government, to conduct winding up of banking companies, though the Central Government may notify that a High Court need not have one. Official liquidator (Section 39): the Reserve Bank, the State Bank or another bank notified, or an individual named in the application, may be appointed official liquidator by the High Court on the Reserve Bank application. The liquidator makes a preliminary report within two months of the winding up order on the availability of assets for preferential payments and discharge of liabilities and gives notice calling for claims within fifteen days. Depositors need not make claims (Section 43): the claim of each depositor is deemed filed for the amount in the books of the bank. Preferential payment (Section 43A): the liquidator makes certain preferential payments first, in addition to Section 327 of the Companies Act, to depositors in savings accounts up to a limit; the balance goes to general creditors and then to further amounts due to depositors; the provision does not apply to deposits covered by deposit insurance. Voluntary winding up (Section 44): permitted only if the Reserve Bank certifies that the bank will be able to pay all its debts in full as they accrue; the High Court may order winding up by the court, during voluntary winding up, if it becomes clear that the bank cannot meet its debts or voluntary winding up is detrimental to the interests of depositors.

Penalties (courseware): a banking company must abide by the Reserve Bank Act, the Banking Regulation Act and the rules, directions and regulations under them; non-compliance invites penalties. Reserve Bank Act, Chapter V: false statements in an application, return or statement, known to be false or wilfully omitting a material statement, are punishable with imprisonment up to three years and also a fine; failure to produce books or documents is punishable with a fine and, for continuing offences, a daily fine; Sections 58B(3) to 58B(5B) deal with contravention of Chapter IIIB directions including Sections 31, 45E and 45J. Offences by companies: every person in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business is deemed guilty unless proved the offence was committed without knowledge or with due diligence; a court takes cognizance of an offence under the Act (other than Chapter IIIC deposit offences) only on a complaint by an officer of the bank generally or specially authorised in writing; a metropolitan magistrate or a first class judicial magistrate tries the offences. Banking Regulation Act: Section 46 deals with penalties for false statements, failure to produce documents or information, contravention of Section 35(4)(a) (deposits taken in contravention of an order, punishable with fine up to twice the deposits taken) and other contraventions or defaults with fine and, for continuing contravention, a further daily fine; Section 47: cognizance only by a metropolitan magistrate or judicial magistrate of the first class (or superior) on a complaint of an officer of the Reserve Bank (and in some cases the National Bank); Section 47A: the Reserve Bank may itself impose a penalty for default or contravention; if it exercises this power, no complaint is filed in court for the same contravention or default.

Held back as not verified and not asked in any question: every rupee amount of fine and penal interest in the penalty sections (fines of Rs 1 crore, Rs 20 lakh, Rs 50 thousand a day, Rs 1 lakh a day under the Banking Regulation Act; Rs 1 lakh and Rs 5,000 a day under the Reserve Bank Act), the Rs 250 preferential payment limit in winding up, the date by which a foreign bank must display its accounts, and the courseware statement that the Banking Companies (Nomination) period of preservation of records is five to eight years.

facts.statement: State Bank of India (courseware): the State Bank of India was established under Section 3 of the State Bank of India Act, 1955 to take over the undertaking of the Imperial Bank and to carry on the business of banking and other business in accordance with the Act. It is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal and can sue and be sued in its name. The majority of shares are held by the Government of India and no shareholder other than the Government can exercise voting rights above ten per cent unless otherwise specified by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank. Its central office is the corporate centre in Mumbai; local head offices are in Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and other places decided by the Central Government in consultation with the Central Board. The Central Board has general superintendence and direction; it works on business principles with regard to public interest. The Central Government can give directions on matters of policy involving public interest in consultation with the Governor of the Reserve Bank and the Chairman of the State Bank, and the directions are given through the Central Board. The Board makes regulations to carry out the Act, in consultation with the Reserve Bank and with the prior sanction of the Central Government. Composition: a Chairman, not more than four Managing Directors appointed by the Central Government, and other directors appointed to represent workmen and officers, nominated by the Central Government from persons with special knowledge of co-operatives and rural economy, and elected by shareholders other than the Reserve Bank. The Chairman and Managing Directors hold office for a period not exceeding five years and are eligible for reappointment; the Central Government can terminate service with three months notice or pay in lieu after consulting the Reserve Bank. Local boards are set up at each place where there is a local head office (Section 21B). Business: the State Bank acts as agent of the Reserve Bank at places where it has a branch and the Reserve Bank does not, to transact Government business; apart from this it carries on banking as defined in Section 5(b) and business under Section 6(1) of the Banking Regulation Act and may acquire other banks with the sanction of the Central Government or if so directed. Accounts and audit: the books are closed and balance sheets prepared each year on 31 March; within three months the balance sheet and profit and loss account with the auditors report and a report by the Central Board on the working and activities of the State Bank are furnished to the Central Government and the Reserve Bank. The audit is by a person qualified under Section 226 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 141 of the 2013 Act); no director, member of a local board, committee or officer of the bank is eligible; the appointment is by the Reserve Bank with the previous approval of the Central Government; the auditors report and the report of the Central Board are laid before Parliament; within two months particulars of the shareholders as on that date are sent to the Government and the Reserve Bank; the annual general meeting is held within six weeks of sending the balance sheet. Subsidiary banks: there were seven subsidiary banks; State Bank of Saurashtra and State Bank of Indore were merged earlier, and on 15 February 2017 the Central Government approved the merger of five associate banks (State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur, State Bank of Hyderabad, State Bank of Travancore, State Bank of Mysore, State Bank of Patiala) and Bharatiya Mahila Bank with SBI with effect from 1 April 2017. The Central Government may make rules under Section 49 and the State Bank may make regulations with the approval of the Reserve Bank.

Regional Rural Banks (courseware): Regional Rural Banks were set up from 1975 under the Regional Rural Banks Ordinance, 1975, replaced by the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976, because the ethos and attitude of the existing banks were not fully conducive to the credit needs of rural people. The preamble describes the object as developing the rural economy by providing credit and other facilities for agriculture, trade, commerce, industry and other productive activities in rural areas, particularly for small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans and small entrepreneurs. Section 3 authorises the Central Government to establish a Regional Rural Bank by notification at the request of a sponsor bank, to operate within specified local limits; the sponsor bank holds 35 per cent of the issued capital, the Central Government holds 50 per cent and the State Government holds the remaining fifteen per cent as the courseware states. Every RRB is a body corporate with perpetual succession and a common seal; it is generally allotted a compact area of operation of a few districts with homogeneous agro-climatic and rural conditions; it can accept all types of deposits from the public and engage in banking as in Section 5(b) of the Banking Regulation Act. Management vests in the board of directors, which works on business principles with due regard to public interest; the board makes regulations to give effect to the Act in consultation with the sponsor bank and with the previous approval of the Central Government, which can give directions on matters of policy involving public interest. The board consists of a chairman appointed by the sponsor bank from among its officers in consultation with NABARD or otherwise by the Central Government in consultation with NABARD; the chairman is whole-time and removable by the sponsor bank in consultation with NABARD and in other cases in consultation with the Central Government. A person who is adjudicated insolvent or convicted of an offence involving moral turpitude is disqualified as a director, and absence from three consecutive board meetings without leave of the board results in vacation of office. Business: an RRB may carry on Section 5(b) banking and business under Section 6(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, but the main business is granting loans and advances to small and marginal farmers, agricultural labourers, artisans, small entrepreneurs, agricultural marketing societies, farmers service societies and self-help groups within the notified area. Accounts and audit: books are closed on 31 March or another date the Central Government specifies; auditors with the approval of the Central Government qualified under Section 226 of the Companies Act, 1956 (Section 141 of the 2013 Act); the auditors report and report on the working are laid before Parliament; the sponsor bank is empowered to monitor the progress of the RRBs by inspection, internal audit and scrutiny. Amalgamation: two or more RRBs may be amalgamated by the Central Government by notification, with provision for continuation of service of employees, binding on all parties; since 2012-13 amalgamation and consolidation were carried out to cut overheads and widen operations.

Nationalised banks (courseware): apart from SBI, the other public sector banks are called nationalised banks because they came into being through the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and 1980 (the Bank Nationalisation Acts), by which the undertakings of 20 existing private banks were transferred to the corresponding new banks. The whole paid-up capital was taken over by the Central Government; later most were listed after public issues. The 2006 Amendment (Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) and Financial Institutions Laws (Amendment) Act, 2006) lets the banks raise capital by public issue, preferential allotment or private placement of equity or preference shares, but the Central Government must hold not less than fifty-one per cent of the equity at all times, and no shareholder other than the Central Government may exercise voting rights above one per cent of total voting rights. Each nationalised bank is a body corporate with perpetual succession, can sue and be sued, and carries on banking as in Section 5(b) and other business in Section 6(1) of the Banking Regulation Act; with SBI and private banks they act as financial supermarkets through branches or subsidiaries. The board has general superintendence, direction and management of affairs and follows policies laid down by the Reserve Bank and the Central Government; the Central Government may issue directions on public interest matters in consultation with the Governor of the Reserve Bank. Section 9 of the Acts empowers the Central Government to make schemes in consultation with the Reserve Bank; the schemes (Nationalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme, 1970 and 1980) are laid before Parliament, are binding, and deal with constitution of the board, appointment of chairman and managing director, terms of whole-time directors, disqualification and vacation of office, board meetings, committees, increase in paid-up capital and other matters. Section 19 empowers the board to frame regulations with the consent of the Reserve Bank and Central Government. Directors appointed or nominated by the Central Government: a Chairman and Managing Director (in bigger banks a separate Chairman and a Managing Director and CEO); not more than four other whole-time directors; one director who is an official of the Central Government; one director with expertise in regulation or supervision of commercial banks nominated on the recommendation of the Reserve Bank; one representing workmen employees; one representing officers; one chartered accountant with at least fifteen years of experience nominated in consultation with the Reserve Bank; and up to six other directors nominated by the Central Government. Shareholders other than the Central Government may elect up to three directors. Fit and proper criteria apply to every director and the Reserve Bank notified in 2019 stricter fit and proper directions for elected directors. Meetings (Section 12 of the Schemes): at least six times a year and at least once in each quarter; the meeting may be held by video conferencing or other electronic means; ordinarily not less than fifteen days notice; business other than that for which the meeting was convened requires the consent of the Chairman and a majority of directors present unless one weeks written notice was given to the Chairman; the quorum is one-third of the directors holding office. Committees (Sections 13 and 13A and 14): the Management Committee and the Credit Approval Committee have powers delegated by the board; other committees may be constituted to advise.

Banking Regulation Act and public sector banks (courseware): Section 51 of the Banking Regulation Act lists the sections of the Act applicable to the State Bank, nationalised banks (corresponding new banks) and Regional Rural Banks; the other sections are not applicable because the State Bank Act and the Nationalisation Acts contain provisions which modify or override them. The applicable sections (as tabulated in the courseware) include: Section 10 (prohibition of employment of managing agents and restrictions on certain forms of employment); Sections 13 to 15 (restriction on commission, brokerage and discount on sale of shares, prohibition of charge on unpaid capital, restrictions on payment of dividend); Section 17 (reserve fund); Sections 19 to 21A (restrictions on subsidiaries, RBI power to regulate advances and similar); Sections 23 to 28 (restrictions on opening and transfer of places of business, maintenance of a percentage of assets); Section 29 except sub-section 3 (accounts and balance sheet); Section 29A (associate enterprises); Section 30(1B), (1C) and (2) (special audit and auditors); Section 31 (submission of returns); Section 34 (accounting provisions not retrospective); Section 35 (inspection by the Reserve Bank); Section 35A (directions); Sections 35AA and 35AB (insolvency resolution directions and directions on stressed assets); Section 36 except 1(d); Sections 45Y to 45ZF (preservation of records, return of paid instruments, nomination for deposits, lockers and safe custody); Sections 46 to 48 (penalties, cognizance of offences, imposition of penalties); Section 50 (claims for compensation barred); Section 52 (rule-making power); Section 53 (power of the Government to exempt). Disinvestment: the State Bank of India Act was amended by the State Bank of India (Amendment) Act, 1993 so that capital is divided into shares of Rs 100 each, and the restriction on voting rights (two hundred votes) was changed to up to ten per cent. The Nationalisation Act of 1970 (and 1980) was amended in 1994 and 1995 for public holding of shares: the authorised capital could be Rs 1,500 crore divided into shares of Rs 10 each, with authority to increase or reduce between Rs 1,500 crore and Rs 3,000 crore, voting rights of shareholders limited to one per cent per shareholder, a register of shareholders, and Section 10A amended to allow dividends with earlier balance of profits to be transferred. The courseware also describes the August 2019 mega merger of 10 public sector banks into four, effective 1 April 2020, and a Government move to privatise.

Co-operative banks: applicability (courseware): co-operative banks are registered under State co-operative societies laws or under the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act; a bank operating only in one State is governed by the State law and a bank operating in more than one State is governed by the Central Act; the State or Central law governs constitution and related matters, but banking business is regulated by the Banking Regulation Act as applicable to co-operative societies, subject to modifications in Part V (Section 56), made applicable by the Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1965. Section 5(cci) defines a co-operative bank as a State co-operative bank, a central co-operative bank and a primary co-operative bank. A primary co-operative bank means a co-operative society, other than a primary agricultural credit society, which satisfies: (i) its primary object or principal business is the transaction of banking business; (ii) the paid-up share capital and reserves are not less than Rs 1 lakh; (iii) its bye-laws do not permit admission of any other co-operative society as a member except by subscribing to the share capital out of funds provided by the State Government. A State co-operative bank is the principal co-operative society in a State with the primary objective of financing other societies; a central co-operative bank is the principal society in a district with the primary objective of funding other co-operative societies in the district. A reference to a banking company in the Act is read as a reference to a co-operative bank. Name: no co-operative society other than a co-operative bank may use bank, banker or banking as part of its name, and a co-operative bank must use at least one of these words; exempt are a primary credit society, a society formed for the protection of mutual interests of co-operative banks or land development banks, and a co-operative society formed by employees of the State Bank, a subsidiary, a nationalised bank or a co-operative bank (other than a primary credit society) or of a primary credit society or land development bank. Paid-up capital and reserves: not less than Rs 1 lakh to commence or carry on banking business (Section 11 as applicable); this does not apply to a primary credit society which becomes a primary co-operative bank, for two years, extendable by one year; the real and exchangeable value of paid-up capital and reserves counts and the Reserve Bank decision on a dispute is final. Cash reserve: co-operative banks other than scheduled co-operative banks and scheduled State co-operative banks maintain in India by way of cash reserve with itself or by way of balance in a current account with the Reserve Bank or with the State or district central co-operative bank, an amount not less than three per cent of demand and time liabilities in India on the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight; for scheduled primary co-operative banks and State co-operative banks the reserve is as per Section 42 of the RBI Act. Restrictions on loans (Section 20 as applicable): no loans on the security of own shares; no unsecured loans or advances to any of its directors; no unsecured loans to firms or private companies in which a director is partner, managing agent or guarantor, or to individuals where a director is guarantor; and no unsecured loans to a company in which the chairman is managing agent or chairman or managing director. The courseware notes that these restrictions do not apply to unsecured loans against bills for supplies to Government or bills of exchange arising from bona fide trade transactions; and that from 1 October 2003 the Reserve Bank prohibited co-operative banks from providing, renewing secured or unsecured loans and advances or any other funded or non-funded financial accommodation to their directors and their relatives and to firms or companies in which relatives are interested.

Co-operative banks: licensing, liquid assets, accounts, inspection and deposit insurance (courseware): a co-operative society needs a licence from the Reserve Bank under Section 22 (as applicable) to carry on banking business, but primary credit societies are exempt; societies carrying on banking at the commencement of the 1965 Act were exempt for a period of one year, had to apply for a licence within three months of commencement, and a primary credit society that becomes a primary co-operative bank applies within three months of becoming one; after applying, it can continue until its licence is rejected. Branches: prior permission of the Reserve Bank to open a new place of business or change its location except within the same city, town or village; temporary branches up to one month at an exhibition, conference or mela are allowed; opening or changing location of branches by a central co-operative bank within its area of operation is exempt; the application of a co-operative bank for permission to open a branch, other than a primary co-operative bank, is routed through NABARD with an advance copy to the Reserve Bank. Liquid assets (Section 24(1) as applicable): co-operative banks maintain liquid assets; balances with the Reserve Bank or with a State co-operative bank and central co-operative bank are counted; Section 24(2A) liquid assets not less than 25 per cent or other percentage not exceeding forty per cent as the Reserve Bank may notify, maintained at the close of business on any day; a return is filed with the Reserve Bank and, other than by a primary co-operative bank, a copy to NABARD. Accounts: the balance sheet and profit and loss account are prepared as at the last working day of the year in the forms in the Third Schedule; three copies with the statutory auditor report are submitted to the Reserve Bank within six months; a State co-operative bank and a central co-operative bank submit such return to NABARD also. Inspection: Section 35 applies with minor modifications; the Reserve Bank may call for inspection of a primary co-operative bank by officers of the State co-operative bank in the State where the primary bank is registered, and may supply a copy of the inspection or scrutiny report to the State co-operative bank or the Registrar of Co-operative Societies. Deposit insurance: the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961 applies to co-operative banks; under Section 13C co-operative banks must be registered with the corporation; the registration may be cancelled if the bank is prohibited from accepting deposits, its licence is cancelled, it is ordered wound up, it has ceased to be an eligible co-operative bank, it has converted into a non-banking co-operative society, it is amalgamated with another co-operative bank, or it has transferred its deposit liabilities. An eligible co-operative bank under Section 2(gg) is one whose law provides that an order for winding up, or sanctioning a scheme of compromise, arrangement, amalgamation or reconstruction, can be made only with the previous sanction in writing of the Reserve Bank, that a winding up order may be made if the Reserve Bank requires, and that supersession of the board and appointment of an administrator for a period not exceeding five years in aggregate is made if the Reserve Bank requires; the liquidator, insured bank or transferee must repay the Corporation under Section 21. Section 13D: the Reserve Bank may requisition winding up of a co-operative bank if it fails to comply with Section 11 capital requirements, its licence is cancelled, it is prohibited from taking fresh deposits under Section 35(4) or Section 42(3A)(b) of the RBI Act, it continues to contravene the Act after notice, it is unable to pay its debts, or a compromise cannot be worked or its continuance is prejudicial to depositors. A co-operative bank is deemed unable to pay its debts if on the returns the Reserve Bank is of opinion that it is unable to pay, or if it refused a lawful demand within two working days where the Reserve Bank has an office, branch or agency, or within five working days elsewhere, and the Reserve Bank certifies it cannot pay.

Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 (courseware): the Act was enacted on 29 September 2020 but is deemed to have come into force on 26 June 2020, except Section 4, which, in so far as it relates to primary co-operative banks, is deemed to have come into force on 29 June 2020, and in so far as it relates to State co-operative banks and central co-operative banks, comes into force on a date the Central Government notifies (with different dates possible). The Act replaced the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Ordinance, 2020 and brought 1,482 urban and 58 multi-State co-operative banks under the supervision of the Reserve Bank. Salient features: the Reserve Bank may initiate a scheme for reconstruction or amalgamation of a bank, including a co-operative bank (Section 45); once the Reserve Bank imposes a moratorium on a bank it cannot grant any loans or make investments in any credit instruments during the moratorium (amended Section 45(3)); co-operative banks may issue equity, preference or special shares on face value or at a premium to members or persons residing in their area of operations, and unsecured debentures or bonds with maturity of ten years or more, but prior approval of the Reserve Bank is required (Section 56 as applied to Section 12); no person is entitled to demand payment on surrender of shares issued to him (Section 12 as applied); the Reserve Bank may exempt a co-operative bank or a class from specified provisions mainly relating to employment, qualification of the board and appointment of a chairman, by notification (Section 53A); and the Reserve Bank may supersede the board of a multi-State co-operative bank for up to five years in the public interest and to protect depositors (new Section 36AAA).

Private sector banks (courseware): private sector banks are those in which the majority stake is held by private individuals or entities; they are mostly incorporated under the Companies Act and bound by the Banking Regulation Act and the Reserve Bank Act. There are two categories: old private sector banks that came into existence before 1968 and new private sector banks incorporated after the 1990s (the courseware counts 21 banks as at 31 March 2021). Many new banks have thrived because they were free from baggage, started with a clean slate and used advanced technology to provide error-free, quick and efficient services to a mostly affluent clientele. Most of the bigger private banks established after the 1990s were set up under the Companies Act and follow the Banking Regulation Act along with the former statute.

Differentiated banks (courseware): differentiated banks are those that cater to the needs of a specific sector or a certain demographic segment of the population; they function in a niche segment and may be defined as those that offer a limited range of services or functions under a different regulatory dispensation, or differ in capital requirement or scope of activities or area of operations. The concept was first discussed in 2007; urban co-operative banks, primary agricultural credit societies, regional rural banks and local area banks existed before 2007 and may be considered differentiated banks as they operate in localised areas. The Reserve Bank discussion paper Banking Structure in India: The Way Forward (August 2013) suggested a transition path to a differentiated bank model. The Committee headed by Shri Nachiket Mor (Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low-Income Households) proposed two designs: the Horizontally Differentiated Banking System (HDBS), in which banks specialise in one or more of payments, deposits and credit, and the Vertically Differentiated Banking System (VDBS), in which a full-service bank gives all services but is differentiated on size, geography or sector. Niche institutions exist in other countries (for example postal savings in South Korea, GE Capital for credit and payments, MasterCard and Visa for payments only). Advantages: unlocking of specialisation, long-term infrastructure lending needing high risk management expertise, very low ticket unsecured credit, filling gaps in MSME financing through asset and cash flow based lending, operating leases and factoring, customised risk management and regulatory compliance, and better price discovery and reduced intermediation cost. Payments banks: the Reserve Bank issued the key features of payments banks in November 2014 with the objectives of providing small savings accounts and payments and remittance services to migrant labour workforce, low income households, small businesses and other unorganised sector entities; eligible promoters include non-bank pre-paid payment instrument issuers, individuals or professionals, non-banking finance companies, corporate business correspondents, mobile telephone companies, supermarket chains and companies, real sector co-operatives and public sector entities; the promoter or group should be fit and proper with a sound track record of professional experience for at least five years; payment banks may accept demand deposits, issue ATM and debit cards but not credit cards, provide payment and remittance services, act as business correspondent of another bank and distribute simple non-risk sharing financial products such as mutual funds and insurance products; they cannot undertake lending activities; they invest at least 75 per cent of demand deposit balances in SLR eligible Government securities or treasury bills of maturity up to one year and hold a maximum of 25 per cent in time or fixed deposits with other scheduled commercial banks; they must maintain the cash reserve ratio; a payments bank has the minimum paid-up equity capital of Rs 100 crore and a leverage ratio of not less than 3 per cent; the promoter contribution is 40 per cent for the first five years (all figures as in the 2014 and 2016 circulars and recorded in the courseware as dated). Small finance banks: the November 2014 guidelines aimed at furthering financial inclusion by providing savings vehicles and supplying credit to small business units, small and marginal farmers, micro and small industries and unorganised sector entities through high technology and low cost operations; the bank primarily does basic banking of acceptance of deposits and lending to unserved and underserved sections; there is no restriction on area of operations; the minimum paid-up equity capital is Rs 100 crore; the promoter contribution is at least 40 per cent initially, brought down to 26 per cent within 12 years; they are subject to cash reserve and statutory liquidity requirements as for other scheduled commercial banks and must lend 75 per cent of adjusted net bank credit to priority sectors with at least 50 per cent of the loan portfolio in loans up to Rs 25 lakh. The courseware also records 2019 on-tap licensing guidelines and the August 2022 permission to act as authorised dealer category-I.

Local Area Banks (courseware): in 1996 a decision was taken to allow the establishment of Local Area Banks in the private sector to bridge gaps in credit availability and enhance the institutional credit framework in rural and semi-urban areas and provide efficient and cost-effective financial intermediation services. The minimum start-up capital was expected to be Rs 5 crore with promoters bringing the entire minimum share capital up-front; the NRI contributions to equity and the holding by a family among the promoter group should not exceed 40 per cent of the capital within three years from the date of licensing; the voting rights of an individual shareholder are restricted to ten per cent under Section 12(2) of the Banking Regulation Act. Norms: the area of operation is usually restricted to a maximum of three geographically contiguous districts; LABs finance agriculture and allied activities, small scale industries, agro-industrial activities, trading and non-farm sectors and comply with norms regarding lending to MSME, priority sector and weaker sections; they are registered as public limited companies under the Companies Act, as partnership firms under the Partnership Act, or as limited liability partnerships, are licensed under the Banking Regulation Act and may be included in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act; they are subject to prudential norms, accounting policies and other policies laid down by the Reserve Bank; supervision lies with the relevant department of the Reserve Bank; at the time of grant of licence a LAB may open a branch in a single urban centre in each district and the remaining branches in rural and semi-urban centres. Their main function is to aid the development of the area, to provide all types of normal universal banking services and to mobilise rural savings. Of about 227 applications in 1996, the Reserve Bank approved only 10 licences; the courseware states that only two were in existence as at January 2022 (Coastal Local Area Bank Ltd, established 27 December 1999, head office Vijayawada, covering Krishna, Guntur and West Godavari districts; and Krishna Bhima Samruddhi Local Area Bank Ltd, established 28 February 2001, head office Mahbubnagar, covering Mahbubnagar, Raichur and Gulbarga districts). Their importance has become limited after the opening of differentiated banks such as small finance banks.

facts.statement: NBFC and its regulators (courseware): a Non-Banking Financial Company is a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956 (2013) engaged in the business of loans and advances, acquisition of shares, stocks, bonds, debentures or securities issued by government or a local authority or other marketable securities of a like nature, leasing, hire-purchase, insurance business or chit business, but does not include any institution whose principal business is that of agriculture activity, industrial activity, purchase or sale of any goods (other than securities) or providing any services and sale, purchase or construction of immovable property. The Department of Non-Banking Supervision of the Reserve Bank regulates and supervises NBFCs under Chapter III B and C and Chapter V of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The focus of regulation is threefold: depositor protection, consumer protection and financial stability. The Reserve Bank can take punitive action including cancellation of the certificate of registration, prohibitory orders on accepting deposits, filing criminal cases or winding up petitions under the Companies Act in extreme cases. Because many NBFCs have become systemically significant, the Reserve Bank introduced a revised scale based regulatory framework by circular RBI/2021-22/112 of 22 October 2021, effective from 1 October 2022.

Role of NBFCs in inclusive growth (courseware): NBFCs historically provide small ticket personal loans, financing of two and three wheelers, truck financing, farm equipment, loans for used commercial vehicles and machinery, and working capital finance, and are suited to micro, small and medium enterprises because of simpler processes and quicker, friendlier and flexible repayment aligned to their clients, albeit at a higher cost. They supplement the role of banks and are financial intermediaries delivering credit to the unorganised sector and small local borrowers. Activities: credit to MSMEs, micro finance institutions (NBFC-MFIs, providing loans, savings, money transfer and micro insurance to poor people), gold loan NBFCs (loans against gold jewellery, simplified sanction and quick disbursement), second hand vehicle financing (very popular with road transport operators), and affordable housing (small ticket loans to home buyers in low income segments, with relaxed documentation). NBFCs aid economic development by mobilisation of resources, capital formation, provision of long-term credit and specialised credit, aid in employment generation, help in development of financial markets and in attracting foreign grants and in breaking the vicious circle of poverty by serving as government instrument. The courseware stresses that although NBFCs do not include certain business, in India NBFCs are bound by banking rules and regulations of the Reserve Bank.

Registration (courseware): under Section 45-IA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 every NBFC must be registered with the Reserve Bank to commence or carry on any business of a non-banking financial institution; Section 45-IA(1) requires a certificate of registration from the Reserve Bank and a net owned fund of twenty-five lakh rupees or such other amount, not exceeding one hundred crore rupees, as the Reserve Bank may notify (different amounts may be notified for different categories); the Reserve Bank has specified two crore rupees as the net owned fund required for an NBFC to commence or carry on business except where a specific requirement is prescribed. To avoid dual regulation, certain categories regulated by other regulators are exempt from registration with the Reserve Bank: venture capital funds, merchant banking companies and stock broking companies registered with SEBI; insurance companies holding a valid certificate of registration issued by IRDAI; Nidhi companies notified under Section 620A of the Companies Act, 1956; chit fund companies under the Chit Funds Act, 1982; housing finance companies regulated by the National Housing Bank; stock exchanges; and mutual benefit companies. The Master Direction of 1 September 2016 sets out applicable NBFC categories: systemically important non-deposit taking NBFCs, deposit taking NBFCs, NBFC-Factors (registered under Section 3 of the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011), NBFC-Infrastructure Debt Fund, NBFC-Micro Finance Institutions, NBFC-Infrastructure Finance Companies and others, each subject to conditions on asset size, net owned fund and credit rating that the courseware quotes as at its writing.

Revised scale based regulatory structure (courseware): NBFCs are divided into four layers based on size, activity and perceived riskiness: Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer and Top Layer. The Base Layer comprises non-deposit taking NBFCs below the asset size of Rs 1,000 crore and NBFCs undertaking peer to peer lending (NBFC-P2P), account aggregator (NBFC-AA), non-operative financial holding companies (NOFHC) and NBFCs not availing public funds and not having a customer interface. The Middle Layer comprises all deposit taking NBFCs irrespective of asset size, non-deposit taking NBFCs with asset size of Rs 1,000 crore and above, and NBFCs undertaking the activities of standalone primary dealers, infrastructure debt fund NBFCs, core investment companies, housing finance companies and infrastructure finance companies. The Upper Layer comprises NBFCs specifically identified by the Reserve Bank as warranting enhanced regulatory requirement, based on parameters and a scoring methodology; the top ten eligible NBFCs in terms of asset size always reside in the Upper Layer, irrespective of any other factor. The Top Layer would ideally remain empty and may be populated only if the Reserve Bank is of the opinion that there is a substantial increase in the potential systemic risk from specific NBFCs in the Upper Layer. Public funds include funds raised directly or indirectly through public deposits, inter-corporate deposits, bank finance and all funds received from outside sources such as borrowings and debentures but exclude funds raised by issue of instruments compulsorily convertible into equity shares within a period not exceeding five years. Customer interface means interaction between the NBFC and its customers while carrying on its business. Nomenclature: from 1 October 2022 NBFC-ND and NBFC-D references change (the courseware text says NBFC-ND, NBFC-ND-SI and NBFC-D become NBFC-BL or NBFC-ML).

Net owned funds and asset norms for applicable NBFCs (courseware): net owned fund (NOF) requirements differ by category (for example peer to peer and account aggregator Rs 2 crore, infrastructure debt fund Rs 300 crore, core investment companies, housing finance companies Rs 20 crore, infrastructure finance companies Rs 300 crore, mortgage guarantee companies Rs 100 crore, with different requirements by 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2027 for investment and credit companies, micro finance institutions and factors). Provisioning for standard assets for NBFCs classified as NBFC-UL, with effect from 1 October 2022: individual housing loans and loans to small and micro enterprises 0.25 per cent; housing loans at teaser rates 2.00 per cent decreasing to 0.40 per cent after one year from the date the rates are reset at higher rates if accounts remain standard; advances to commercial real estate residential housing sector 0.75 per cent; advances to commercial real estate other than residential housing 1.00 per cent; restructured advances as per the applicable prudential norms; and all other loans and advances not included above, including loans to medium enterprises, 0.40 per cent; current credit exposures on permitted derivative transactions attract provisioning as for standard assets. NPA classification: the NPA recognition norm changes to overdue for more than 90 days for all categories of NBFCs, with a glide path for those in the Base Layer not already at 90 days: more than 150 days overdue by 31 March 2024, more than 120 days by 31 March 2025, and more than 90 days by 31 March 2026. Board experience: at least one director shall have relevant experience of having worked in a bank or NBFC. Ceiling on IPO funding: Rs 1 crore per borrower for financing subscription to initial public offer, with NBFCs free to fix more conservative limits.

Capital and prudential guidelines (courseware): for NBFC-ML and NBFC-UL, internal capital adequacy assessment (ICAAP) requires a thorough internal assessment of the need for capital commensurate with the risks in business, on similar lines to Pillar 2 for commercial banks; it is not to be insisted on in the Pillar 2 sense, and covers credit, market, operational and other residual risks with methodology proportionate to the scale and complexity of operations. Additional regulatory changes for NBFC-UL: Common Equity Tier 1 of at least 9 per cent of risk weighted assets, a leverage requirement (ceiling to be prescribed), and differential provisioning for different classes of standard assets. Every applicable NBFC shall maintain a minimum capital ratio consisting of Tier I and Tier II capital not less than 15 per cent of its aggregate risk weighted assets on balance sheet and risk adjusted value of off-balance sheet items; Tier I capital at any point of time shall not be less than 10 per cent for applicable NBFCs other than NBFC-MFI and IDF-NBFC; NBFCs primarily lending against gold jewellery (loans comprising 50 per cent or more of their financial assets) shall maintain a minimum Tier I capital of 12 per cent. Concentration of credit or investment: the extant separate limits are merged into a single exposure limit of 25 per cent for a single borrower or party and 40 per cent for a single group of borrowers or parties, measured with reference to Tier I capital instead of owned fund (earlier limits: lending 15 and investment 15 per cent for a single party, total 25; group 25 and 25, total 40, as a percentage of owned fund). The ceiling on investment in shares of another company does not apply to an insurance company up to the extent specifically permitted in writing by the Reserve Bank; an applicable NBFC may exceed the concentration norms by 5 per cent for a single party and 10 per cent for a single group if the additional exposure is on account of infrastructure loan or investment; infrastructure finance companies may exceed by 10 per cent of owned fund for a single borrower and 15 per cent for a single group of borrowers. Sensitive sector exposure: exposure to capital market (direct and indirect) and commercial real estate; NBFCs fix Board approved internal limits for sensitive sector exposure and a sub-limit within the commercial real estate exposure ceiling for financing land acquisition. Regulatory restrictions on loans: loans and advances to directors, their relatives and to entities where directors or their relatives have major shareholding, and to senior officers of the NBFC are restricted; for real estate proposals, borrowers must have obtained prior permission from government or local authorities for the project wherever required, and disbursement is made only after requisite clearances. A Large Exposure Framework is introduced for NBFCs in the Upper Layer with large exposures to counterparties and groups of connected counterparties considered for exposure ceilings. NBFC-UL must also determine internal exposure limits on other important sectors and have a Board approved limit for exposure to the NBFC sector.

Corporate governance of NBFCs (courseware, base layer onwards): NBFCs are required to constitute a Risk Management Committee (RMC) at Board or executive level to evaluate the overall risks including liquidity risk and report to the Board; disclosure requirements expanded to include types of exposure, related party transactions, loans to directors and senior officers, and customer complaints; NBFC-BL need a Board approved policy on loans to directors, senior officers and their relatives; Key Managerial Personnel except for directorship in a subsidiary shall not hold any office, including directorship, in any other NBFC-ML or NBFC-UL (with a two year timeline from 1 October 2022), though they can assume directorship in NBFC-BLs; an independent director shall not be on the Board of more than three NBFCs (NBFC-ML or NBFC-UL) at the same time, with the Board ensuring no conflict; there is no restriction on directorship on Boards of NBFC-BLs subject to the Companies Act, 2013. Disclosures in annual financial statements with effect from 31 March 2023: corporate governance report with composition and category of directors and shareholding of non-executive directors, modified opinion of auditors, items of income and expenditure of exceptional nature, breaches in terms of covenants in respect of loans availed or debt securities issued, and divergence in asset classification and provisioning above a threshold to be decided by the Reserve Bank. Chief Compliance Officer: NBFCs appoint a CCO sufficiently senior in the hierarchy and put in place a Board approved policy laying down the role and responsibilities of the CCO. Compensation: a Board approved compensation policy including a Remuneration Committee and principles for fixed and variable pay. Other governance matters: the Board shall delineate the role of committees (Audit Committee, Nomination and Remuneration Committee, Risk Management Committee) and lay down a calendar of reviews; a whistle blower mechanism for directors and employees; good governance practices in subsidiaries; and NBFCs with 10 and more branches are mandated to adopt a Core Banking Solution with a glide path of three years from 1 October 2022.

Fair practices (courseware): applicable NBFCs having a customer interface shall adopt guidelines on loan applications and their processing: all communications to the borrower in the vernacular language or a language understood by the borrower; loan application forms with necessary information affecting the interest of the borrower so that a meaningful comparison with the terms and conditions offered by other NBFCs can be made and an informed decision taken, indicating the documents required with the application form; and a system of giving acknowledgement for receipt of all loan applications, preferably indicating the time frame within which loan applications will be disposed of.

Bank finance to NBFCs and co-lending (courseware): most aspects relating to financing of NBFCs by banks have been deregulated, but restrictions on financing certain activities continue. Terms: current investments are investments classified as current assets in the balance sheet of the borrower and intended to be held for less than one year; long term investments are all other investments; unsecured loans are loans not secured by any tangible asset; Residuary Non-Banking Companies (RNBCs) are companies classified and registered with the Department of Non-Banking Supervision as such. NBFCs not requiring registration: insurance companies registered under Section 3 of the Insurance Act, 1938, Nidhi companies notified under Section 620A of the Companies Act, 1956, chit fund companies carrying on chit fund business as their principal business as per the Explanation to clause (vii) of Section 45-I(bb) of the RBI Act, stock broking and merchant banking companies registered under Section 12 of the SEBI Act, and housing finance companies regulated by the National Housing Bank. The ceiling on bank credit linked to the net owned fund of NBFCs has been withdrawn for all NBFCs statutorily registered with the Reserve Bank and engaged in principal business of asset financing, loan, factoring and investment activities; banks may extend need based working capital facilities and term loans and may extend finance to second hand assets financed by NBFCs with the approval of their Boards within prudential guidelines. For Residuary Non-Banking Companies bank finance is restricted to the extent of their net owned fund. Activities not eligible for bank credit include: bills discounted or rediscounted by NBFCs except rediscounting of bills discounted by NBFCs arising from sale of commercial vehicles (including light commercial vehicles) and two wheeler and three wheeler vehicles subject to conditions that the bills should have been drawn by the manufacturer on dealers only, represent genuine sale transactions as ascertained from the chassis or engine number, and the bank satisfies itself of the bona fides and track record of the NBFC; investments of NBFCs in both current and long-term nature, in any company or entity by way of shares, debentures and so on, though stock broking companies may be provided need-based credit against shares and debentures held by them as stock in trade; unsecured loans and inter-corporate deposits by NBFCs to or in any company; all types of loans and advances by NBFCs to their subsidiaries, group companies or entities; finance to NBFCs for further lending to individuals for subscribing to initial public offers and for purchase of shares from the secondary market. Co-lending model (CLM): banks and NBFCs shall formulate Board approved policies for entering into the co-lending model and place them on their websites; under the CLM a Master Agreement may be entered into between the two partner institutions covering the criteria for selection of partner institutions, specific product lines and areas of operation, terms and conditions, and segregation of responsibilities and customer interface and protection issues; the Master Agreement may provide for either an irrevocable commitment by the bank to take its share of individual loans originated by the NBFC in its books or the retention of discretion to reject certain loans after due diligence; banks shall comply with the Master Direction on Know Your Customer and the guidelines on outsourcing, and may not rely on due diligence by third parties for KYC in an unsupervised manner; where the bank exercises discretion, the arrangement is akin to a direct assignment transaction and must comply with the guidelines on transactions involving transfer of assets through direct assignment of cash flows (minimum holding period exemption applies only where a back-to-back basis clause exists); and banks shall not be allowed to enter into co-lending arrangements with an NBFC belonging to the promoter group.
